newsitem.title: BOSNIA: Bosnian Serb leader takes oath of office.
newsitem.headline: Bosnian Serb leader takes oath of office.

text.p: Bosnian Serb President Biljana Plavsic pledged reluctant respect on Saturday for Bosnia's integrity and said she would work with Moslems and Croats in the country's post-war government.

She told the inaugural session of new Bosnian Serb parliament in Banja Luka that "we are not entirely independent, that our sovereignty is limited and that we are obliged to abide by what has been signed."
Plavsic, heard by international mediators, said Serbs were being forced "to live within a state which is not to our liking."

Under the peace agreement reached almost a year ago, Bosnia has been divided into two loosely-linked halves, a Bosnian Serb republic and a Moslem-Croat federation which regard each other with mistrust.
Despite the Serbs' failure to win independence, Plavsic hailed "the beginning of a new era in (Serb) statehood."
Moslem members of the Bosnian Serb parliament refused to swear an oath of office but joined their former foes in a minute of silence for the 200,000 dead of the Bosnian war.
Fourteen of the 18 Moslems elected to the assembly and a Croat deputy left the session while Serbs took the oath expressing loyalty to the Bosnian Serb republic and to the Christian religion.
They returned to listen to Plavsic's speech, which marked a significant step forward to the creation of joint institutions.
Momcilo Krajisnik, the Serb member of the collective Bosnian presidency, also swore his oath of office after previously resisting doing so.

Krajisnik, retiring speaker of the parliament, said Moslems who did not want to take the oath could refer it to the assembly's judicial committee which would issue a binding decision on the legality of its wording.
A spokesman for Bosnian President Alija Izetbegovic protested against the religious elements in the Bosnian Serb oath and the version of the presidency oath taken by Krajisnik.
Mediators were expected to put pressure on both sides to compromise for the sake of getting inter-ethnic government bodies to work.
The Banja Luka building where the parliament met was hung with crucifixes and Serbian Orthodox clergy sat with Bosnian Serb leaders.
Despite their objections to the heavy religious symbolism, the Moslems stood with Serb deputies when they sang the Serb nationalist hymn "God give us justice."
The religious ceremony was also boycotted by Bosnian Serb former communist deputies who refused to kiss the cross or receive blessing from the Orthodox metropolitan.
When he called the minute's silence, Krajisnik said it was in memory of all the dead of the 3-1/2 year war, the great majority of whom were Moslems.
The Serb parliament was elected in September at the same time as a national assembly which has its seat in Sarajevo and represents all three Bosnian national communities.
Thousands of Moslems and Croats were driven out of the Banja Luka area in northern Bosnia during the war and several of Bosnia's oldest mosques were blown up.
